newsitem.title: FRANCE: France plans tighter rules on hostile takeovers.
newsitem.headline: France plans tighter rules on hostile takeovers.

text.p: French Finance Minister Jean Arthuis announced plans for tighter takeover rules on Thursday to help companies fend off hostile bids, in France's latest move to modernise its corporate sector.

The changes, which allow companies more time to defend themselves, reflect a shift from traditional cosy practices where companies were protected by cross-shareholdings and state intervention, to modern procedures allowing them to compete in Europe's more open single market.
Arthuis told a news conference that the government was also putting the final touches on another of its big reforms, introducing private pension funds.
"My objective is for everything to be in place by the end of June," he said, without giving further details.

France already has an ambitious privatisation programme which is expected to fuel interest in the stock market. The launch of pension funds is also expected to boost company capital and channel savings into shares.

On takeover rules, Arthuis said the Paris market's top watchdog body, the Financial Markets Council, had proposed extending the period in which a bid runs to 25 days for an agreed offer and 35 days for hostile bids from 20 for both now.
The extension will give companies more time to defend themselves, if necessary through a capital increase, against hostile bids from either French or other European companies.

Arthuis said the COB stock market watchdog had also proposed lowering the shareholding threshold at which a company must declare its intentions about any future bid to 10 percent from 20 percent, an idea he said he favoured.

The proposals follow a call last year by President Jacques Chirac for improved takeover rules. Chirac argued that French companies were too exposed compared with their principal competitors. They were also more vulnerable to takeovers since they were less heavily capitalised, he said.
French firms have long been protected by an elaborate system of cross-shareholdings, where company heads basically packed the board with friends from other French companies.
These shareholdings are now being unravelled as companies sell off non-stategic assets to focus on their bottom line.
Hostile bids have been rare in France, as elsewhere in mainland Europe, although German steelmaker Krupp's KFHG.F unwelcome bid this week for its larger rival Thyssen may indicate changes on the way.

French plans for better takeover rules reflect a move across Europe to end traditional practices protecting companies and replace them with tighter procedures more in line with those in the United States or Britain.

In Britain bids usually run for 60 days. In theory companies can make a takeover in 21 days but this has been unsuccessful in the past. Britain also has tight rules limiting the speed at which companies can build up share stakes.

The new rules also reflect a drive by the conservative government to reform the corporate sector and channel funds via tax reforms into an efficient stock market, which it sees as the key to shifting savings into industry and jobs.
The new pension funds, which will be encouraged through tax breaks, are expected to invest largely in stocks, seen as providing a higher return in the long term.
They will be set up by agreement between employers and employees, run alongside the current system of universal state pensions and managed by banks and insurers.
Analysts have said they expect the impact on the stock market, currently dwarfed by the giant bond market, to be relatively slow as companies take the time to set up funds.
But some in the business estimate flows of up to 30 billion francs ($5 billion) a year when the system is fully up and running.
($ = 5.686 French Francs)
